label: Temple Scroll 11Q19 (Megillat HaMikdash) — Part 2 — Col 23–44
summary_plain: The middle section of the Temple Scroll continues with the architecture of the outer court, the buildings, and the purity regulations for the Temple city. The outer court is vast — large enough for all Yisra’el to assemble. Chambers are designated for specific priestly functions. Detailed purity laws govern who may enter each court and when. The scroll describes the slaughtering places, the drains, and the storage for sacred vessels. Regulations for the king are given: the king shall not multiply horses, he shall not take many wives, he shall write a copy of the Torah and read it all the days of his life. The king’s guard is composed of twelve thousand warriors from all the tribes.
summary_scholarly: Columns 23-44 of the Temple Scroll cover the outer Temple architecture, the purity regulations, and the Law of the King (columns 56-59, with its foundation laid in this section). The outer court dimensions create a sacred precinct far larger than the Second Temple’s actual footprint. The purity regulations are stricter than both the Masoretic Torah and later rabbinic halakhah. The Law of the King rewrites Devarim 17:14-20 with significant expansions: the king’s council of thirty-six (twelve priests, twelve Levites, twelve Yisra’elites), the prohibition against taking foreign wives, the king’s obligation to consult the high priest, and the standing army of 12,000. The text presents an alternative constitutional order for Yisra’el that limits royal power through priestly oversight and tribal representation.

key_terms.definition: Columns 13-29 of the Temple Scroll describe a festival calendar based on the 364-day solar year — including standard Torah festivals plus additional first-fruits festivals for wine, oil, and wood not found in the standard festival list of Vayikra/Devarim.

An additional festival in the Temple Scroll's calendar — 50 days after Shavuot (Feast of Weeks), the New Wine festival celebrates the first fruits of the vine. This is not in the standard Torah festival list; the Temple Scroll expands the calendar.

Another additional festival in the Temple Scroll — 50 days after the New Wine festival, celebrating the first fruits of olive oil. Part of the Temple Scroll's expanded first-fruits framework that applies the Shavuot pattern to wine and oil.

The Temple Scroll specifies a festival for bringing wood to the Temple (cols 23-25) — a 6-day ceremony where each tribe brings its assigned wood offering on appointed days. This corresponds to a Nehemiah 10:35 reference but is elaborated in the Temple Scroll far beyond any other ancient text.

The Temple Scroll's festival calendar expands the Shavuot (Feast of Weeks) pattern — counting 50 days from one festival to the next — to generate the New Wine and New Oil festivals. The result is a calendar that fills the summer months with covenant celebration.

The Temple Scroll's expanded first-fruits framework: not just grain (Shavuot) but wine and oil are presented to YHWH as first-fruits, with their own 50-day counting cycles. Every agricultural product flows to YHWH first before the community uses it.

Columns 45-51 of the Temple Scroll contain detailed purity laws governing who may enter the Temple city, how long various impurities last, and the rules for cleansing. Part 2 (cols 23-44) transitions from the festival calendar into the purity framework.

The Temple Scroll defines a 'holy city' (ir hamikdash) with specific boundaries — a designated area around the Temple within which stricter purity rules apply. The city of the Temple is not just the Temple mount but a larger sacred zone.

The Temple Scroll coordinates the sacrificial offerings for each festival with the 364-day solar calendar — specific offerings on specific days, in specific quantities, following the Torah's festival laws but organized by the solar calendar framework.

The Temple Scroll's Part 2 is organized by the 364-day solar calendar — festivals always fall on fixed weekdays, the Wood Festival and first-fruits festivals fill the calendar with covenant celebration, and the purity laws are timed to the calendar's structure.

faq.question: What additional festivals does the Temple Scroll add to the standard Torah calendar?
faq.answer: The Temple Scroll adds three major festivals not in the standard Torah festival list of Vayikra 23 and Devarim 16: the New Wine Festival (50 days after Shavuot), the New Oil Festival (50 days after New Wine), and the Wood Festival (a 6-day ceremony for tribal wood offerings, mentioned briefly in Nehemiah 10:35 but massively elaborated here). These festivals fill the summer months between Shavuot and the autumn feasts — using the 50-day counting pattern of Shavuot applied to wine and oil.

faq.question: How does the 50-day pattern work in the Temple Scroll's calendar?
faq.answer: Shavuot (Feast of Weeks) is defined by counting 50 days from the day after the Sabbath following Passover. The Temple Scroll takes this 50-day counting structure and extends it: New Wine arrives 50 days after Shavuot; New Oil arrives 50 days after New Wine; and the Wood Festival follows. This creates a chain of festivals through the summer, each 50 days apart, organized by the 364-day solar calendar so that each festival falls on a fixed weekday every year.

faq.question: What is the Wood Festival?
faq.answer: A 6-day ceremony in which each of the twelve tribes brings its assigned portion of wood to the Temple. The wood is used for the altar fires — the Temple requires a continuous supply of fuel for the daily burnt offerings. The brief reference in Nehemiah 10:35 mentions a wood offering but gives no detail. The Temple Scroll elaborates it into a full week-long tribal ceremony with assigned days for each tribe or family group. This shows the community's attention to the practical logistics of Temple service.

faq.question: What is the first-fruits theology in the Temple Scroll?
faq.answer: The Temple Scroll's principle: every agricultural product belongs to YHWH first. Grain has Shavuot's first-fruits offering. Wine has the New Wine festival. Oil has the New Oil festival. This comprehensive first-fruits framework means the community cannot use any major agricultural product — grain, wine, oil — until it has first been presented to YHWH in a festival context. The creation's produce flows to YHWH before flowing to the community. This is not mere ritual; it is a statement about who owns the land's abundance.

faq.question: How does the Temple Scroll's calendar differ from the Jerusalem Temple's calendar?
faq.answer: The Jerusalem Temple used a lunar calendar, meaning its festivals fell on different days of the week from year to year. The Temple Scroll uses the 364-day solar calendar — festivals always fall on fixed weekdays. Beyond the fixed/variable calendar difference, the Temple Scroll adds New Wine, New Oil, and Wood festivals that the Jerusalem Temple did not observe. For the community, this meant the Jerusalem Temple was celebrating YHWH's feasts on the wrong days and missing entire festivals YHWH had commanded.

faq.question: What is the holy city (ir hamikdash) concept?
faq.answer: The Temple Scroll designates a large zone around the Temple as the 'holy city' — a sacred area with stricter purity regulations than the city of Yerushalayim as a whole. Within this holy city zone, more activities are restricted, impurities are more serious, and special rules govern who may sleep inside it, what may be done there, and how purification works. This concept expands the sacred geography: holiness does not stop at the Temple gate but radiates outward into a designated urban zone.

faq.question: How does the Temple Scroll's expanded festival calendar connect to the community's covenant identity?
faq.answer: The expanded festivals — New Wine, New Oil, Wood — are covenant celebrations: they bring every major agricultural product before YHWH, affirm tribal identity through the Wood Festival's tribal assignments, and use the summer months (normally a gap in the festival calendar) for covenant celebration. A community that observes these festivals is a community that acknowledges YHWH's ownership of the land's abundance in every product, throughout every season. The expanded calendar is a comprehensive covenant life, not just an annual cycle of seven standard feasts.

faq.question: What connects the Temple Scroll's festival calendar to 4QMMT and 1 Chanokh?
faq.answer: All three texts — the Temple Scroll, 4QMMT, and 1 Chanokh's Astronomical Book — share the 364-day solar calendar. The festival calendar dispute in 4QMMT (which lists the solar calendar in Section A as the first dispute with Jerusalem) is the same calendar that governs the Temple Scroll's festivals and that 1 Chanokh's Astronomical Book describes cosmologically. The solar calendar was not a minor preference — it was the foundational covenant issue that the community considered worth separating from Jerusalem over.

faq.question: How does the Temple Scroll's purity geography work?
faq.answer: The Temple Scroll creates a series of nested purity zones: the innermost court (priests only), the middle court (Levites and pure Yisra'elite males), the outer court (women, purifying individuals, resident aliens), the Temple mount, and the larger holy city zone. Each zone has its own rules about who may enter and what disqualifies entry. This graduated geography maps covenant holiness spatially — the closer to YHWH's presence, the more intense the purity requirement. The structure is not punitive but architectural: it reflects the structure of holiness itself radiating outward from YHWH's dwelling.

faq.question: Why is the Wood Festival significant?
faq.answer: The Wood Festival represents something otherwise absent from the standard festival calendar: a ceremony specifically organized by all twelve tribes together, each with an assigned day and role. The twelve-tribe participation in a shared annual ceremony is a statement about Yisra'el's corporate covenant identity — the whole community, through all its tribal divisions, participates together in sustaining YHWH's altar. This tribal unity through covenant service is the Wood Festival's theological point, beyond its practical function of supplying altar wood.
